children.text: Evolution of a supermassive black-hole binary

Use Newtonian point masses except for the supplied gravitational radiation law. Each black hole has mass M≫m, every star has m=M☉, and the holes eventually form a binary with each circular orbital radius a, separation 2a. Use G=\(6.67\times10^{-11}\) SI, c=\(3.0\times10^{8}\) m/s, M☉=\(2.0\times10^{30}\) kg, 1 pc=\(3.1\times10^{16}\) m and cosmic age tH=13.7 Gy. Give distances in pc and times in Gy. Estimates may differ by up to a factor ten, while tasks saying find require exact expressions within the given model. In A stars initially rest with uniform density ρ=mn in a galaxy of size R. The hole moves at v and b1=GM/v². In B stars far from the binary have speed σ≪vbin and density ρ. A star reaching distance about a is ejected at speed about vbin. In C use exactly the supplied radiation model \(\dot E=-(1024/5)(G/c^5)(\omega^3I)^2\), with I=2Ma² and ω=vbin/a. This coefficient is part of the exercise model. In D set M=\(10^{8}\)M☉, σ=200 km/s, R=20 kpc and stellar density ρ(r)=σ²/(4πGr²).

children.text: Evolution of a supermassive black-hole binary
Integrate the transverse gravitational impulse along the undeflected straight path. It gives Δp⊥=2GMm/(bv), hence α=2GM/(bv²)=2b1/b and k=2.
The star keeps its speed in the hole frame. To order α², its longitudinal momentum change has magnitude mvα²/2. The hole receives drag \(\Delta p_x=-mv\alpha^2/2=-2G^2M^2m/(b^2v^3)\).
The rate in an annulus db is 2πbvn db. Therefore \[F_{DF}=-\frac{4\pi G^2M^2\rho}{v^2}\ln\frac R{b_1}.\] The negative sign is relative to the velocity. The logarithm comes from db/b.
Angular momentum gives bσ=rmvp. Energy gives vp²=σ²+2GM2/rm. Thus \(b=r_m\sqrt{1+2GM_2/(\sigma^2r_m)}\).
Use M2=2M and rm≈a. Strong focusing gives bmax²≈4GMa/σ². The rate πbmax²nσ gives \(\Delta t\simeq m\sigma/(4\pi GM\rho a)\). This approximate cross section sets the numerical convention used below.
Each ejected star takes approximately mvbin²/2=GmM/(8a). Divide by the B3 interval: \(\dot E\simeq-\pi G^2M^2\rho/(2\sigma)\). Since dE/da=GM²/(4a²), \(\dot a\simeq-2\pi G\rho a^2/\sigma\).
Integrate da/a²=−(2πGρ/σ)dt. The halving time is \(T_{SS}=\sigma/(2\pi G\rho a_1)\simeq7.3\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Gy}\).
Using ω²=GM/(4a³) and I=2Ma² yields \(\dot E=-64G^4M^5/(5c^5a^5)\). Divide by dE/da=GM²/(4a²): \(\dot a=-256G^3M^3/(5c^5a^3)\).
Integration gives \(T_{GW}=5c^5(a_2^4-r_g^4)/(1024G^3M^3)\simeq5c^5a_2^4/(1024G^3M^3)\). The approximation neglects rg⁴.
The enclosed stellar mass is M*(r)=σ²r/G. Therefore v²=GM*(r)/r=σ² and v=σ.
Circular kinetic energy is constant, while dU/da=Mσ²/a. The energy-loss rate is FDFσ=−GM²σlnΛ/a². Thus \(\dot a\simeq-GM\ln\Lambda/(a\sigma)\).

A mass-equivalence estimate M*(a1)≈M gives \(a_1\simeq GM/\sigma^2\simeq10.8\,\mathrm{pc}\). Equating the actual forces instead gives GM/(4σ²)≈2.7 pc. Both are legitimate within the source's estimate criterion. Use the 10.8 pc convention consistently below.
Integrate D2: \(T_1=\sigma(a_0^2-a_1^2)/(2GM\ln\Lambda)\simeq0.121\,\mathrm{Gy}\). The a1² correction is negligible.

Equate the B4 and C1 energy-loss magnitudes. Then \[a_2^5=\frac{128G^2M^3\sigma}{5\pi c^5\rho_1}.\] For a1=10.8 pc, ρ1≈\(6.3\times10^{3}\)M☉/pc³ and a2≈0.018 pc. The alternative 2.7 pc formation convention gives a2≈0.010 pc.

\[T_2\simeq\frac\sigma{2\pi G\rho_1}\left(\frac1{a_2}-\frac1{a_1}\right)\simeq0.063\,\mathrm{Gy},\quad T_3\simeq\frac{5c^5a_2^4}{1024G^3M^3}\simeq0.016\,\mathrm{Gy}.\] At the transition T3≈σ/(8πGρ1a2), one quarter of the dominant term in T2. The alternative a1 convention gives 0.0068 and 0.0017 Gy.

Add T1+T2+T3≈0.121+0.063+0.016=0.20 Gy. The alternative force-equivalence estimate gives approximately 0.13 Gy. Both use the stated replenished stellar population approximation. Depletion of stars on intersecting orbits would invalidate a constant slingshot rate, the final-parsec issue mentioned in the source.

solution.text:
Evolution of a supermassive black-hole binary
a.1. Weak scattering coefficient
Integrate the transverse gravitational impulse along the undeflected straight path. It gives Δp⊥=2GMm/(bv), hence α=2GM/(bv²)=2b1/b and k=2.
a.2. Longitudinal impulse
The star keeps its speed in the hole frame. To order α², its longitudinal momentum change has magnitude mvα²/2. The hole receives drag \(\Delta p_x=-mv\alpha^2/2=-2G^2M^2m/(b^2v^3)\).
a.3. Dynamical friction
The rate in an annulus db is 2πbvn db. Therefore \[F_{DF}=-\frac{4\pi G^2M^2\rho}{v^2}\ln\frac R{b_1}.\] The negative sign is relative to the velocity. The logarithm comes from db/b.
a.4. Coulomb logarithm
b1=GM/v²≈10.8 pc, so lnΛ≈ln(20000/10.8)≈7.53.
b.1. Circular binary energy
Use Mvbin²/a=GM²/(4a²). Then \(v_{bin}=\sqrt{GM/(4a)}\) and \(E=2(Mv_{bin}^2/2)-GM^2/(2a)=-GM^2/(4a)\).
b.2. Gravitational focusing
Angular momentum gives bσ=rmvp. Energy gives vp²=σ²+2GM2/rm. Thus \(b=r_m\sqrt{1+2GM_2/(\sigma^2r_m)}\).
b.3. Collision interval
Use M2=2M and rm≈a. Strong focusing gives bmax²≈4GMa/σ². The rate πbmax²nσ gives \(\Delta t\simeq m\sigma/(4\pi GM\rho a)\). This approximate cross section sets the numerical convention used below.
b.4. Slingshot shrinkage
Each ejected star takes approximately mvbin²/2=GmM/(8a). Divide by the B3 interval: \(\dot E\simeq-\pi G^2M^2\rho/(2\sigma)\). Since dE/da=GM²/(4a²), \(\dot a\simeq-2\pi G\rho a^2/\sigma\).
b.5. Radius-halving time
Integrate da/a²=−(2πGρ/σ)dt. The halving time is \(T_{SS}=\sigma/(2\pi G\rho a_1)\simeq7.3\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Gy}\).
c.1. Radiative shrinkage
Using ω²=GM/(4a³) and I=2Ma² yields \(\dot E=-64G^4M^5/(5c^5a^5)\). Divide by dE/da=GM²/(4a²): \(\dot a=-256G^3M^3/(5c^5a^3)\).
c.2. Radiative merger time
Integration gives \(T_{GW}=5c^5(a_2^4-r_g^4)/(1024G^3M^3)\simeq5c^5a_2^4/(1024G^3M^3)\). The approximation neglects rg⁴.
c.3. Hubble-time radius
\(a_H=[1024G^3M^3t_H/(5c^5)]^{1/4}\simeq0.098\,\mathrm{pc}\).
d.1. Galaxy circular speed
The enclosed stellar mass is M*(r)=σ²r/G. Therefore v²=GM*(r)/r=σ² and v=σ.
d.2. Frictional orbital decay
Circular kinetic energy is constant, while dU/da=Mσ²/a. The energy-loss rate is FDFσ=−GM²σlnΛ/a². Thus \(\dot a\simeq-GM\ln\Lambda/(a\sigma)\).
d.3. Binary formation radius
A mass-equivalence estimate M*(a1)≈M gives \(a_1\simeq GM/\sigma^2\simeq10.8\,\mathrm{pc}\). Equating the actual forces instead gives GM/(4σ²)≈2.7 pc. Both are legitimate within the source's estimate criterion. Use the 10.8 pc convention consistently below.
d.4. Initial sinking time
Integrate D2: \(T_1=\sigma(a_0^2-a_1^2)/(2GM\ln\Lambda)\simeq0.121\,\mathrm{Gy}\). The a1² correction is negligible.
d.5. Transition to radiation
Equate the B4 and C1 energy-loss magnitudes. Then \[a_2^5=\frac{128G^2M^3\sigma}{5\pi c^5\rho_1}.\] For a1=10.8 pc, ρ1≈\(6.3\times10^{3}\)M☉/pc³ and a2≈0.018 pc. The alternative 2.7 pc formation convention gives a2≈0.010 pc.
d.6. Late-stage durations
\[T_2\simeq\frac\sigma{2\pi G\rho_1}\left(\frac1{a_2}-\frac1{a_1}\right)\simeq0.063\,\mathrm{Gy},\quad T_3\simeq\frac{5c^5a_2^4}{1024G^3M^3}\simeq0.016\,\mathrm{Gy}.\] At the transition T3≈σ/(8πGρ1a2), one quarter of the dominant term in T2. The alternative a1 convention gives 0.0068 and 0.0017 Gy.
d.7. Total evolution time
Add T1+T2+T3≈0.121+0.063+0.016=0.20 Gy. The alternative force-equivalence estimate gives approximately 0.13 Gy. Both use the stated replenished stellar population approximation. Depletion of stars on intersecting orbits would invalidate a constant slingshot rate, the final-parsec issue mentioned in the source.
